newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian politicians agree change after mass rally.
newsitem.headline: Belgian politicians agree change after mass rally.

text.p: Belgian politicians threw their weight behind constitutional change on Monday in response to mass protests against widespread corruption.

All major parties voiced backing for a proposal made on Sunday by Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene to remove an article from the constitution that gives all political parties representation in the judiciary.
Sunday's rally brought a quarter of a million people out onto the streets of the capital.
The size of the protest took everyone -- organisers, police, the government and the king -- by surprise, as did the fact that it passed without serious incident.
Meddling by politicians in the promotion of magistrates and lawyers has been seen as the root of what is widely deemed to be a corrupt and morally-bankrupt legal system.

The protests, joined by people from all over Belgium, was supposed to be a show of support for the parents of children who have been abducted, sexually abused and -- in at least four cases -- killed by a gang that is widely believed to have high-level protection.
But it was equally a demonstration of deep public anger at the system as a whole, although political analysts said the resulting changes would be largely cosmetic.

On Monday a scattering of student demonstrations followed a week of protests. They were prompted by the removal of magistrate Jean-Marc Connerotte from investigations into a murderous paedophile ring led by convicted rapist Marc Dutroux.
Some 120 bus, tram and metro drivers from the Brussels transport authority also stopped work.
"Yesterday we took people to the demonstration, today it is our turn to protest. We know promises have been made, we just want to prove we are vigilant," one told Belgian television.
Foreign Minister Erik Derycke, on a state visit to Japan with King Albert, said the king had been amazed by the large turnout on Sunday and by the dignity of the marchers.
The monarch welcomed the solidarity shown by Belgians from all ages and walks of life, the minister said.
Dehaene also promised on Sunday that nothing would be allowed to hinder the child sex abuse investigations.

That may satisfy some people for a while, but changes will have to be made -- a point Dehaene accepted when he said on Sunday he would be meeting with the parents of some of the dead an missing children before the year end to assess progress.

But so widely are the tentacles of political power spread that it will be accelerated evolution not revolution in a nation where politicians spend much of their time setting the French and Dutch-speaking halves of country against each other.

"There were no political objectives on Sunday, just expressions of anger," Helmut Gaus, Professor of Political Science at Ghent University and the author of many books on politics and social change, told Reuters in an interview.
"People will forget very quickly," he said, noting that a general election was not due for another two-and-a-half years.
"You have to see it in the historical context. We are now at the bottom of a 25-year cycle so we have maximum anxiety in our society...But we are already rising out of the trough," he said.
"Connerotte and all that is a pretext for the masses to show empathy with a dramatic scene. But the political consequences of that will not be very extensive," Gaus added.
